summaries.example: Imagine a story about a round square. A round square cannot exist in the ordinary world, but the story may still talk about one. An impossible world is a tool for describing a way things could not really be. It can help us ask what else would be true in that strange story.
summaries.summary:
We often talk about ways the world could be different. Philosophers call these possible worlds. We also talk about ways the world could not be: for example, a situation in which a shape is completely round and completely square, or in which a logical rule fails. The entry studies these impossible worlds. They are not necessarily imaginary places. They may be models, descriptions, or other devices for representing impossible situations.

There are several kinds. One kind includes any way things absolutely could not be. A narrower kind breaks a logical law. An even narrower kind contains both a statement and its denial, such as “the lamp is on” and “the lamp is not on.” Philosophers can also make the idea relative: what counts as a rule may differ from one world-description to another.

Why use such strange tools? A person’s beliefs may include mistakes or small conflicts. Information from different witnesses may disagree. A novel may intentionally describe a round square, or accidentally give two different accounts of a character. Impossible worlds can represent these cases without pretending that ordinary reality contains a round square. They can also help us reason from an impossible assumption, such as asking what would follow if a rule of mathematics or logic were different.

The approach has challenges. If anything can happen in an impossible world, it may stop explaining much. Philosophers also ask how such worlds should be built, how similar one impossible world can be to another, and whether meanings of complex sentences can still be made from the meanings of their parts. The entry presents these questions without claiming that one answer has won.
key_ideas: Philosophers use impossible worlds to represent situations that cannot really happen.
Different impossible worlds may break different rules. Some may contain a contradiction, while others may break another logical rule.
Impossible worlds can help explain confused beliefs, mixed information, unusual drawings, stories with mistakes, and reasoning about impossible ‘what if’ questions.
Philosophers disagree about whether impossible worlds are real things or useful descriptions and tools.
summaries.why_it_matters: Impossible worlds give philosophers and computer scientists a way to keep track of ideas that are mistaken, conflicting, incomplete, or impossible. They may help us understand how real people think without assuming that people know every logical consequence of what they believe. They also help explain how a fictional story can contain a contradiction while still having a meaningful plot. Their usefulness is debated, so studying them also teaches us how models can help—and where models may fail.

important_terms.definition: A complete way things might be, used by philosophers to think about possibility.
A described way things could not be, perhaps because it breaks logic or another necessary rule.
A rule of thinking, such as the idea that something cannot be both true and false in the same way at the same time.
Information, beliefs, or statements that do not fit together consistently.

questions_to_think_about: Can a story still make sense if it contains a contradiction?
Why might a computer database need to keep two conflicting reports in separate places?
Is every strange situation impossible, or can some merely be unlikely?
Would an impossible world be a real place, a description, or something else?

summaries.example: Suppose a philosopher asks, “If intuitionistic logic were correct, what would follow?” In intuitionistic logic, the Law of Excluded Middle is not accepted in the same unrestricted way as in classical logic. The supposition may be impossible according to classical standards, yet the discussion need not collapse into ‘anything goes.’ One might infer that a certain logical principle fails, while rejecting an unrelated claim about colors. An impossible-world model represents this selective reasoning by including a situation that violates some classical logical rules but preserves enough structure for meaningful conclusions.
summaries.summary:
Possible-worlds theories represent possibility by considering ways things could be. Impossible-worlds theories extend this strategy to ways things could not be. The extension is not a single doctrine. At the broadest level, an impossible world is any absolutely impossible way things might be. Other definitions identify impossible worlds with violations of a chosen logic, violations of classical logic, or situations in which some A and not-A are both true. These definitions form a rough hierarchy: contradiction-realizing worlds are a special case of classical-logic-violating worlds, though not every classical-logic violation is a contradiction.

The entry’s central motivation is explanatory and semantic usefulness. In epistemic and doxastic models, agents may have inconsistent beliefs or may fail to draw every consequence of what they believe. Possible worlds alone tend to generate logical omniscience. Impossible worlds can represent nonideal cognitive states, although completely unconstrained worlds risk collapsing into an arbitrary list of sentences. In information theory and database modeling, reports from separate sources can conflict without every statement being combined into one contradiction. Some impossible worlds are therefore nonadjunctive: A and B may each hold while A-and-B does not. Fiction supplies another application, because a story can contain accidental contradictions or deliberately impossible objects. Impossible worlds can also make propositions more fine-grained. If all impossible propositions are represented by the empty set of possible worlds, distinct contents are lost; impossible worlds can separate them.

key_ideas: The label ‘impossible world’ covers several proposals: ways things cannot be, worlds violating some logic, worlds violating classical logic, and worlds where a statement and its negation are both true.

The main motivation is theoretical utility. Impossible worlds can model intentional states, inconsistent databases, inconsistent or intentional fiction, fine-grained propositional contents, and counterpossible conditionals.
In epistemic logic, impossible worlds can represent agents whose beliefs are inconsistent or not closed under every logical consequence, addressing aspects of logical omniscience.
Different theories disagree about structure. Some impossible worlds preserve ordinary conjunction and disjunction; others are ‘open’ and need not obey any nontrivial inference rule.

Metaphysical views range from realist accounts, to abstract or ersatz constructions, to fictionalist approaches. The Parity Thesis says possible and impossible worlds should have the same general kind of metaphysical status, but this is disputed.
Major objections concern defining possibility without circularity, the usefulness of the framework, the treatment of negation, the behavior of counterpossibles, and compositionality.
summaries.why_it_matters: The framework matters because it connects abstract logic with problems about belief, information, fiction, language, mathematics, and metaphysics. It challenges the assumption that useful representation must describe only genuine possibilities. At the same time, its difficulties are instructive: a model must be structured enough to explain differences, but not so unconstrained that it merely records every difference. The debate therefore concerns both what impossibility is and what a good philosophical model should accomplish.

important_terms.definition: A complete way things could have been, often used to analyze possibility, necessity, conditionals, and propositions.
A world or situation that is not possible in an unrestricted sense; it may violate logical, metaphysical, or other necessary constraints.
Reasoning from an antecedent that is not merely false but impossible, as in asking what would follow if a mathematical or logical necessity failed.
The problem that standard possible-world models make agents know all logical consequences of what they know, even when real agents do not.
Information or beliefs containing conflict, such as both a claim and its negation.
A view of propositions as sets of worlds where they are true; adding impossible worlds can distinguish propositions that agree at every possible world.
The principle that a complex expression’s meaning is determined by the meanings and arrangement of its parts.
A position in which worlds are treated as useful fictional objects rather than as items that belong literally in one’s ontology.

questions_to_think_about: Should an impossible-world model preserve some logical rules, or should it allow every rule except the most basic identity inference to fail?
Does representing an inconsistent belief require a genuinely inconsistent world, or only a special information structure?
Why might a conditional with an impossible antecedent be informative rather than automatically true?
Can impossible worlds distinguish two propositions that have no possible-world difference without making meaning too fine-grained?
What is gained, and what is lost, when worlds are treated as fictional or abstract tools rather than literal entities?

summaries.example: Imagine a group project with two sources of information. One student’s notes say, “The school play is on Friday,” while another’s say, “The school play is not on Friday.” A normal logic system might combine these into a large contradiction. An impossible-world model can keep the reports in separate sections. It represents the conflict without saying that every unrelated statement—such as “the cafeteria is open”—must also be true.
summaries.summary:
We regularly imagine ways things might have been different. Philosophers call these possible worlds. The idea of impossible worlds asks us to consider ways things could not have been, such as a world in which a shape is both completely round and completely square. These worlds are usually tools for representing or reasoning about impossibilities, not ordinary places we can visit.

The entry describes several meanings of ‘impossible.’ Some philosophers use the term for any way things absolutely could not be. Others focus on worlds where a chosen logic fails. A narrower proposal concerns failures of classical logic, while an even narrower one concerns contradictions in which both A and not-A hold. The choice matters because a world can violate a metaphysical rule without violating a logical rule. For example, a world where a famous painting was made by someone other than its actual historical painter might be impossible in one sense but not because of a contradiction in logic.

Why introduce these unusual worlds? Models of knowledge and belief that use only possible worlds often make agents logically omniscient: if an agent knows A and A entails B, the model says the agent knows B. Real thinkers can miss consequences and can hold inconsistent beliefs. Impossible worlds can represent those limitations. They can also model databases containing incompatible reports, fictional works with accidental or intentional inconsistencies, and perceptual experiences such as impossible drawings. In theories of propositions, they help distinguish different impossible contents that would all look identical if we used only possible worlds.

key_ideas: Impossible worlds can be defined in more than one way. They may be any impossible situation, a violation of a selected logic, a violation of classical logic, or a situation containing both A and not-A.
Their value is mainly practical and explanatory: they can model beliefs, inconsistent information, fiction, propositions, and counterpossible reasoning.
A person can have inconsistent beliefs without believing absolutely everything. Impossible worlds can help represent this kind of limited, imperfect thinking.
Not all impossible worlds need be equally chaotic. Some keep ordinary rules for conjunction and disjunction while others allow complex statements to behave independently.
Philosophers disagree about whether impossible worlds are real, abstract constructions, or fictional tools.
Critics ask whether impossible worlds explain anything, how possibility can be defined when impossible worlds are included, and whether meanings remain compositional.
summaries.why_it_matters: Impossible worlds matter because they offer a flexible way to study situations that ordinary logic and ordinary possible-world models handle poorly. They can separate different kinds of error, conflict, and impossibility instead of treating them all as the same. They also show why philosophical models need careful limits: if impossible worlds are too orderly, they cannot represent inconsistency; if they are too chaotic, they may explain nothing.

important_terms.definition: A way the world could be, used to discuss possibility or what might have happened.
A way things could not be, used to represent impossible assumptions, conflicts, or failures of logical rules.
A rule used in reasoning. Different logical systems may accept different rules.
A claim, belief, or set of data that includes a conflict or contradiction.
The mistaken idea that someone who knows a few facts must automatically know every logical result of those facts.
A ‘what if’ statement whose starting point is impossible, not merely untrue.
A theory that treats possible worlds as useful stories or make-believe rather than literal parts of reality.
The idea that the meaning of a complicated sentence comes from the meanings of its smaller parts and their arrangement.

questions_to_think_about: Why might an impossible world be useful even if nobody thinks it is a real place?
Should two conflicting witness reports be combined, or should they remain in separate information groups?
If a story contains an impossible event, does that make every event in the story meaningless?
Can someone reasonably believe two conflicting claims without believing every claim?
Would a world that breaks one logical rule be more similar to our world than a world where every statement is true?
